h1: Mean, Median, Mode, and Range Calculator
description: Free mean, median, mode and range calculator. Paste any dataset and instantly get all four descriptive statistics with step-by-step interpretation.
intro:
Descriptive statistics are the foundation of every data-driven discipline — from elementary-school math homework to clinical research, financial reporting, machine-learning feature engineering and quality control on factory floors. This calculator computes the **four most-used descriptive measures** for any dataset you paste in: the **mean** (arithmetic average), the **median** (the middle value when the data is sorted), the **mode** (the value or values that appear most often), and the **range** (the spread from maximum to minimum).

The formulas are deceptively simple, but knowing **which measure to report matters a lot**. The mean is the only one of the four that uses every data point, so it is sensitive to outliers — a single extreme value can drag it far from the typical observation. The median ignores the magnitude of outliers and reports the 50th-percentile observation, which is why incomes, house prices and salary data are almost always summarized by their median rather than their mean. The mode is the only measure that works on categorical data (favorite color, blood type, brand preference). The range gives you a quick sense of variability but is dominated by extremes; for a more robust spread metric, prefer the interquartile range (IQR) or the standard deviation.

Use this calculator whenever you have a list of numeric values — test scores, daily temperatures, sales figures, response times, sensor readings — and need a fast summary. Paste comma-separated values into the input field (e.g., `2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 11`) and you'll instantly see the four statistics along with an interpretation. The tool handles unsorted input, decimals, negative numbers and duplicate values; it returns multiple modes when the data is multimodal (a tie for most-frequent), and reports "no mode" when every value appears exactly once.

All calculations are performed locally in your browser — your data never leaves your device. The formulas follow the conventions used by NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Wolfram MathWorld, and the standard introductory statistics texts (Triola; Moore, McCabe & Craig). For inferential statistics (confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, regression), descriptive measures are always the first step — start here, then proceed to dedicated inferential calculators.
keyTakeaway: **Mean, median, mode, range**—the four core descriptive statistics. Enter your values and instantly get: the average value, the middle value, the most frequent value, and the data spread (max–min).
useCases: Summarizing a set of 30 student exam scores (e.g., 72, 85, 91, 67, ..., mean = 78.2, median = 79, mode = 85) to report class performance before parent-teacher meetings.

Calculating the mean and median home sale price for a real-estate report covering 50 transactions, where the median ($385,000) better reflects the typical sale than the mean ($432,500) skewed by 3 luxury properties.
Quickly checking daily traffic on a small website over 14 days (e.g., 120, 145, 132, 989, 138, ...) — the range (869) and difference between mean and median flag the day the post went viral.
Computing average response time for a customer-support team over 100 tickets, where the mean (4.8 hours) and median (3.2 hours) reveal a long-tail problem with a few slow-resolution edge cases.
Running a quality-control check on 20 manufactured parts measured for diameter (mm), to flag the most common value (mode) and spot machine drift via the range exceeding the engineering tolerance.
Comparing two months of daily revenue (May vs. June) by mean and median to detect whether revenue grew uniformly or only on a few peak days.
Helping a high-school student verify their statistics homework: given the dataset {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42}, instantly confirm mean = 18, median = 15.5, mode = none, range = 38.

Summarizing 200 patient blood-pressure readings in a clinical trial, where the median systolic pressure is the standard reported metric and the mode highlights any clustering at a treatment threshold.

explanation:
Statistics is one of mathematics' most powerful tools, used across science, engineering, finance, healthcare, and decision-making. Descriptive statistics give you a quick snapshot of what your data looks like.

## How it works

This calculator computes the four most important descriptive statistics:

- **Mean**: The sum of all values divided by the count (the average)
- **Median**: The middle value when data is sorted from smallest to largest
- **Mode**: The value that appears most often in your dataset
- **Range**: The difference between your highest and lowest values

Simply enter your dataset and the calculator instantly shows all four measures.

## Important notes

This calculator is a reference tool for learning and quick analysis. For critical decisions affecting finances, health, or legal matters, consult with a qualified professional. Formulas are current as of 2026 and reviewed regularly.

faq.q: What is the precise difference between mean, median and mode, and when should I use each?
faq.a: The **mean** is the arithmetic average — sum of all values divided by the count. Use it when data is symmetric and outlier-free, and when every observation should influence the result equally. The **median** is the middle value of a sorted dataset (or the average of the two middle values when n is even). Use it for skewed data, income, real-estate prices, response times, and any dataset with outliers — the median is the standard 'typical value' in those contexts. The **mode** is the most-frequent value. Use it for categorical data (favorite product, blood type) or to identify the most common observation when frequency itself matters. For symmetric, unimodal, outlier-free distributions all three converge; for skewed data they diverge, and the choice matters a lot for honest reporting.

faq.q: How exactly do you compute the median when the dataset has an even number of values?
faq.a: Sort the values from smallest to largest. With **n odd**, the median is the value at position (n+1)/2 — the single middle observation. With **n even**, the median is the average of the values at positions n/2 and (n/2 + 1). For example, with the dataset {2, 4, 6, 8} (n = 4), the two middle values are 4 and 6, so the median is (4 + 6)/2 = 5. Note that the median may not be a value that actually appears in the original dataset — this is normal and correct. This convention is the standard in NIST/SEMATECH and is what spreadsheet functions like Excel MEDIAN, Google Sheets MEDIAN, and Python statistics.median return.

faq.q: Can a dataset have more than one mode? What does 'no mode' mean?
faq.a: Yes — a dataset can be **bimodal** (two modes), **trimodal** (three) or more generally **multimodal**. This happens when two or more values are tied for the highest frequency. For example, {1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5} has modes 2 and 4 (each appears twice). A dataset has **no mode** when every value appears exactly once — by some conventions all values are then modes; by others (including this calculator) the dataset is called amodal. Multimodality in real data often signals that the sample is a mixture of two different underlying populations — e.g., a histogram of adult heights bimodal at male and female peaks.

faq.q: What does range mean in statistics, and is it a good measure of variability?
faq.a: The range is simply **maximum − minimum**, the total spread of the data. It is the easiest variability measure to compute and explain, but also the **least robust**: a single outlier (data-entry error, sensor glitch) inflates the range arbitrarily. For most analyses statisticians prefer the **interquartile range (IQR)** = Q3 − Q1, which captures the middle 50% of the data and ignores the extreme 25% on each tail; or the **standard deviation**, which weights every observation by its distance from the mean. Use the range for quick exploratory summaries and for engineering tolerance checks where extremes matter; use IQR or standard deviation for inferential work.

faq.q: Is the mean the same as the 'average'?
faq.a: In everyday speech, yes — when people say 'average' they almost always mean the arithmetic mean. In statistics the word 'average' is a general term that can refer to any measure of central tendency: arithmetic mean, geometric mean, harmonic mean, median or mode. To avoid ambiguity in formal writing, prefer the specific name. The geometric mean (n-th root of the product of n values) is appropriate for rates of growth and ratios; the harmonic mean is appropriate for averaging rates (e.g., average speed across legs of constant distance). For most descriptive purposes 'arithmetic mean' and 'average' are interchangeable.

faq.q: How do outliers affect mean, median, mode and range — and how do I detect outliers?
faq.a: A single extreme outlier can shift the **mean** dramatically — e.g., {1, 2, 3, 4, 1000} has mean 202 but median 3. The **median** is unaffected by outliers as long as fewer than 50% of values are extreme — formally, the median has a **breakdown point of 50%**, the highest of any common statistic. The **mode** is usually unaffected unless the outlier happens to repeat. The **range** is maximally affected — by definition it equals the extremes. To detect outliers, use the IQR rule: any value below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR is a candidate outlier and worth investigating (entry error vs. legitimate extreme observation). Boxplots visualize this immediately.

faq.q: Is this calculator free, and do you store the data I paste in?
faq.a: Yes, completely free with no registration, no paywall, no ads-watching requirement, and no email signup. All calculations run **client-side in your browser** using JavaScript — your data never leaves your device, is not transmitted to any server, and is not logged or stored anywhere. You can safely use this tool with confidential business data, patient records, exam scores or financial figures without privacy concerns. When you refresh or close the tab, all entered data is discarded immediately and irrecoverably. This privacy-by-design approach is consistent across all calculators on Hacé Cuentas and is documented in our public privacy policy.

faq.q: Are the results accurate? What precision does the calculator use?
faq.a: Calculations use **IEEE 754 double-precision floating point**, which gives roughly 15-17 significant digits of accuracy — vastly more than needed for any practical statistical application. The formulas follow standard conventions documented in NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods and used by Excel, Google Sheets, R and Python NumPy. Results match those tools to the displayed precision. For a dataset of more than ~10⁶ values, beware that floating-point summation introduces tiny rounding error in the mean (visible at the 10⁻¹² level); the median and mode are exact regardless of dataset size.

faq.q: What is the difference between sample mean and population mean? Does it matter for this calculator?
faq.a: For the **mean** itself, no — the formula is the same: sum / count. The distinction matters for variability measures like variance and standard deviation, where the sample formula divides by (n − 1) (Bessel's correction) while the population formula divides by n. This calculator computes the **arithmetic mean** of whatever data you paste, treating it as the entire collection of interest. If you are inferring properties of a larger population from a sample, the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean, and you can use the sample standard deviation (n − 1 in the denominator) — but those are inferential statistics, computed separately.

faq.q: How should I handle missing values, text entries, or blanks in my dataset?
faq.a: This calculator expects **numeric values separated by commas, spaces or new lines**. Blanks and non-numeric tokens are silently skipped — they don't count toward n, mean, median, mode or range. In practice you should decide on a missing-data policy *before* calculating: (1) **list-wise deletion** (skip rows with any missing value) is what this tool does by default; (2) **mean imputation** (replace missing values with the dataset mean) is acceptable for exploratory work but biases inferential analyses; (3) **multiple imputation** or model-based methods are best for serious analysis. Never enter 'NA' or '0' as a placeholder for missing — '0' especially distorts every statistic.

faq.q: How does this calculator compare to using Excel, Google Sheets or Python?
faq.a: For descriptive statistics, the results are **identical** — same formulas, same conventions. Use this calculator when you want a fast answer without opening a spreadsheet or writing code, when working from a phone, or when teaching students who don't yet know spreadsheet functions. Use Excel/Sheets when you need to keep the data for further analysis, build charts, or share with colleagues. Use Python (NumPy/Pandas) or R when the dataset has more than ~10⁵ values, when you need reproducibility, or when downstream analysis requires programmatic access. The equivalent functions are: Excel `=AVERAGE()`, `=MEDIAN()`, `=MODE.SNGL()` or `=MODE.MULT()`, `=MAX()-MIN()`; Python `np.mean()`, `np.median()`, `scipy.stats.mode()`, `np.ptp()`.

faq.q: I notice my mean and median are very different — what does that tell me about my data?
faq.a: A large gap between mean and median is a strong signal of **skewness or outliers**. If the mean is much larger than the median, the distribution is **right-skewed** (positive skew) — a few large values pull the mean up. This is typical of income, wealth, response times, file sizes, and city populations. If the mean is much smaller than the median, the distribution is **left-skewed** (negative skew) — a few small values pull the mean down. This is rarer but appears in test scores when most students do well and a few fail. When mean ≈ median, the distribution is roughly symmetric and either statistic is a good summary. As a rule of thumb, if |mean − median| > 0.2 × standard deviation, look at a histogram before reporting.
